source.title: A StrongREJECT for Empty Jailbreaks
source.authors: Alexandra Souly; Qing-Yuan Lu; Dillon Bowen; Tu Trinh; Elvis Hsieh; Sana Pandey; Pieter Abbeel; Justin Svegliato; Scott Emmons; Olivia Watkins; S. Toyer

record.tranche_reason: Tests jailbreak attacks and their effects on harmful-response usefulness, using StrongREJECT scores rather than the original claims' fine-tuning or token-position measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates jailbreak methods on forbidden prompts and reports harmful-response usefulness. It does not test fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples, per-token KL, localization in weights, or training to deepen safety. Figure 3 contains method/model scores, but the extracted numeric layout does not reliably assign values to individual cells; only outcomes stated in the text are recorded. Cited results from other work are not rows.
record.test_reason: Among 37 prompt jailbreaks scored with StrongREJECT on aligned models, the study tests transferred GCG adversarial suffixes and 'prefix injection' (an instruction to start with an affirmative sentence). Both bear on V4's claim that suffixes or a compliant opening defeat refusal. Its other jailbreaks (PAIR, PAP, translation, encodings) are not opening, suffix or decoding attacks. The study does no fine-tuning, KL, localization or deepening work.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that existing benchmarks and evaluators overstate jailbreak effectiveness, and that StrongREJECT agrees best with human judges. They explain the gap by a new finding that jailbreaks bypassing safety fine-tuning tend to reduce capability. They name PAIR and PAP as the genuinely serious threats and say frontier models remain vulnerable to the best per-prompt attack.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates prompt-based jailbreak attacks with a harmful-information usefulness benchmark; does not reproduce fine-tuning, token-position KL, or safety-depth training methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Jailbreak effectiveness varies by method and victim model; GCG works on GPT-3.5 Turbo but not GPT-4o or Llama-3.1 70B. The paper also reports capability costs associated with jailbreak transformations.

fits_no_version.finding: Jailbreaks that most increase aligned models' non-refusal tend to reduce capability: Dolphin's StrongREJECT score and GPT-4o's MMLU score drop.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt jailbreaks that raise willingness tend to degrade response capability.

fits_no_version.finding: LLM-driven rewriting attacks (PAIR, PAP) are the most effective. Per-prompt best-of-37 nearly always achieves a perfect score, while most jailbreaks, including translation, give low-quality responses.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aligned frontier models remain vulnerable to adaptive prompt-rewriting jailbreaks, while many fixed jailbreaks yield little useful harmful content.

record.problems: The StrongREJECT forbidden-prompt dataset contains 313 prompts, which the authors say is not large enough to be a definitive stand-alone robustness measure. Figure 3's extracted numeric layout does not permit reliable assignment of its values to individual methods and models. Human evaluations covered 1,361 labeled data points, and the authors report too few unique jailbreaks for reliable Spearman correlations for GPT-4 and Llama-2.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3 reports scores by jailbreak and victim model, but the extracted flattened layout does not reliably associate individual scores with each method/model cell; those cell-level numeric results were not extracted. Section 3 and Table 1 evaluate automated graders against human judgments, rather than measuring the claim's safety behavior, so their grader-agreement statistics were left out.

untested.parts: Literal prefilling of compliant response tokens; decoding changes (sampling settings); GCG optimized white-box on the target model itself.
All: no per-token KL between aligned and base models.
All: no weight or rank localization.
All: no test of why safety is shallow.

missing.what: Prefix injection (instruction to begin with an affirmative sentence), an opening-based attack bearing on V4. It scores about 0.83 vs 0.14 for None on GPT-3.5 Turbo and about 0.02–0.03 on the other two models.
Per-model numeric GCG and None scores. Values for GPT-3.5 are recoverable; the other two columns' model mapping is uncertain from the flattened text.
missing.locator: Figure 3, GCG (HarmBench), GCG (Universal attacks), None rows

record.verdict_notes: Only GCG and prefix injection bear on V4. Both are tested only in transferred or instruction form, not as literal prefills. The StrongREJECT score mixes willingness and capability, so near-zero scores could partly reflect degraded output rather than refusal. The assignment of Figure 3 columns was inferred: the first column is GPT-3.5 because GCG is high there, matching the text. Whether the second or third column is GPT-4o is unclear, but both are near zero for GCG and prefix injection.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-example fine-tuning intervention or refusal-rate outcome.
No benign-data fine-tuning intervention or harmful-compliance outcome.

Tests several prompt-based jailbreaks, including adversarial suffixes and affirmative-prefix instructions, but not literal prefilled compliant response tokens or decoding changes such as sampling settings.
No weight or rank localization experiment.
No experiment testing why safety would be shallow.
No training intended to distribute safety across response positions or test whether such training holds up.

rows.subject: GPT-3.5 Turbo
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated GCG adversarial suffix jailbreaks on forbidden prompts.

conditions.value: GCG versions (two versions; reported together in the text)

rows.baseline: The paper includes an unmodified-prompt condition, but its value is not stated here.
rows.value: The two GCG versions are described as effective against GPT-3.5 Turbo.
rows.note: The text does not provide the numerical score for this model-method result.
rows.check: State should be observed, not partial. Figure 3's first column, identifiable as GPT-3.5 because it is the only one where GCG scores high, gives GCG (HarmBench) 0.69 and GCG (Universal) 0.84 against 0.14 for None. The baseline and values should be filled in.

source_check.correct: Both GCG variants are described as effective against GPT-3.5 Turbo. Figure 3 reports GCG (HarmBench)=0.69, GCG (Universal attacks)=0.84, and None=0.14.

source_check.problem: The pack truncates the baseline description, preventing complete verification; its note overlooks numerical scores present in Figure 3.

rows.subject: GPT-4o, GPT-3.5 Turbo, and Llama-3.1 70B Instruct (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated 37 jailbreak methods on forbidden prompts.
rows.value: Most tested jailbreaks did not produce high-quality responses to forbidden prompts; observed scores were usually substantially lower than scores reported in the papers that introduced the attacks.
rows.note: This is an aggregate textual characterization, not a reported average.
rows.check: An aggregate over 37 heterogeneous jailbreaks, most unrelated to V4's mechanisms. The comparison is with other papers' reported scores, not a baseline.

rows.subject: GPT-4o, GPT-3.5 Turbo, and Llama-3.1 70B Instruct (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: For each forbidden prompt, selected the most effective jailbreak from those tested.

conditions.value: Best per-prompt choice among tested methods

rows.value: The selected attack could nearly always achieve a perfect StrongREJECT score.
rows.note: This is an adaptive selection over the tested attacks, not the performance of one fixed jailbreak.
rows.check: 'Best' is a per-prompt selection over all methods, i.e. a selection value, not a V4 mechanism. It is also not one fixed attack.

rows.subject: GPT-4-0613
rows.operation_detail: Reproduced the Scots Gaelic translation jailbreak and assessed full generated responses.

conditions.value: Scots Gaelic translation using Google Translate

rows.measure: Whether the response contained useful information about explosives
rows.baseline: The original paper's claimed success case is discussed as the comparison; a matched baseline value is not stated.
rows.value: None of the three outputs provided useful information about explosives.
rows.note: The paper says the outputs resemble the claimed success case initially but do not ultimately provide useful information.
rows.check: A translation jailbreak is not an opening, suffix or decoding attack. It is also a 3-sample qualitative reproduction of a cited result.

rows.subject: Dolphin
rows.operation_detail: Applied jailbreak transformations to forbidden prompts and measured response capability on an unaligned model.
rows.measure: StrongREJECT score on the unaligned model's responses
rows.baseline: No-jailbreak condition is shown in Figure 4; numeric value not stated in the text.
rows.value: Jailbreaks that most successfully increased aligned models' willingness tended to decrease Dolphin's capabilities.
rows.note: This is a capability result on an unaligned model, not a measure of aligned-model refusal or harmful-compliance rate.
rows.check: Capability result on an unaligned model; no V4 bearing.

rows.subject: GPT-4o
rows.operation_detail: Applied jailbreak transformations to benign MMLU questions and measured task performance.
rows.baseline: No-jailbreak condition is shown in Figure 4; numeric value not stated in the text.
rows.value: Jailbreaks that most successfully increased aligned models' willingness on forbidden prompts tended to decrease GPT-4o's MMLU performance.
rows.note: This measures capability on benign prompts, not safety behavior.
rows.check: Capability on benign MMLU; no V4 bearing.

relation.reason: Its own experiments measure whether GCG suffixes produce useful harmful responses from safety-trained models.

tranche.reason: The study evaluates adversarial suffixes and an affirmative-opening instruction using harmful-response usefulness, providing a different method and measure bearing on V4.

source_check.notes: GCG uses transfer from local white-box models; prefix injection requests an affirmative sentence rather than literally prefilling an assistant response. StrongREJECT measures usefulness as well as non-refusal, so low scores alone do not establish that refusal persists.

statements.correction: StrongREJECT: two transferred GCG variants effective against GPT-3.5 Turbo; ineffective against GPT-4o and Llama-3.1 70B according to Section 4. No StrongREJECT numerical result is asserted in this statement. Other studies' numbers are outside this check.
